title: Checkpoint: Breaking the Rules
objective: After this level you can explain how modern artists moved from Post-Impressionism to abstraction and Surrealism.
summary: The chapter in order, from Gauguin's red field to Breton's manifesto, and the 1913 Armory Show that brought modern art to about 300,000 Americans.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: in 1913, America met modern art all at once.
cards.body: Most of this chapter happened in Europe. Then one New York show put it in front of American crowds in a single blast. First, the chapter in order. Then, what happened when the rule-breakers crossed the Atlantic.

events.label: Gauguin paints a vision on a red field

cards.fact: The 1913 Armory Show brought 1,600 works to New York.
cards.context: It ran from February 17 to March 15, 1913, at the 69th Regiment Armory, and about a third of the works were European: a crash course in modern art, from Impressionists to Post-Impressionists and Cubists. Its most famous review was a joke: Duchamp's Cubist painting Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 was popularly called "an explosion in a shingle factory".

cards.headline: Scandal as a delivery system
cards.body: In Chicago, art students hanged Henri Matisse, Walter Pach and Constantin Brancusi (Level 2's Bird in Space) in effigy. Yet the show traveled to New York, Chicago and Boston, and about 300,000 Americans saw it. It pushed young American artists such as Georgia O'Keeffe and Stuart Davis toward new directions. Breaking the rules, it turns out, is contagious.

mascot.line: Being hanged in effigy is rough. Being remembered a century later as the future is a decent consolation.

questions.prompt: At the 1913 Armory Show, which work was mocked as "an explosion in a shingle factory"?

options.label: Van Gogh's The Starry Night
options.rationale: The line was aimed at a Cubist painting.

options.label: Munch's The Scream
options.rationale: The Scream wasn't the target of that joke.

options.label: Magritte's The Treachery of Images
options.rationale: Magritte painted his pipe in 1929, after the show.

questions.explanation: Duchamp's Cubist Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 was popularly called "an explosion in a shingle factory".

questions.prompt: Why does the Armory Show matter in art history?

options.label: It showed Americans European modern art at scale
It was where Impressionism was first shown
It was the show where Dada was founded
It sold Fountain for a record price
options.rationale: Fountain came in 1917 and was refused, not sold.

questions.explanation: About 300,000 Americans saw its European modernism, and it pushed artists like O'Keeffe toward new directions.

questions.prompt: Chapter recap: which of these came last?
questions.explanation: Breton published the Manifesto of Surrealism in 1924, the latest of these.

questions.prompt: Brancusi was hanged in effigy in 1913. What did US customs do with his Bird in Space in 1926 (Level 2)?

options.label: Displayed it at the White House
options.rationale: Customs had no such plans for it.

options.label: Taxed it as metal, not as art
Sent it back to France unopened
options.rationale: It was taxed, then fought over in court.

options.label: Melted it down for scrap
options.rationale: It survived and was ruled art in 1928.

questions.explanation: Customs refused to treat Bird in Space as a sculpture and taxed it as metal. The rule-breakers kept meeting the same question.

questions.prompt: From Level 63: in a pointillist painting, where do the colors blend?

options.label: On the palette, before painting
options.rationale: Seurat avoided mixing on the palette.

options.label: In a glaze brushed over the dots
options.rationale: No glaze; the dots stay separate.

options.label: In the viewer's eye, from a distance

questions.explanation: Pointillist dots of pure color blend visually when you see them from a distance.
